lessons.title: Why water quality matters on the farm
lessons.html:
Water is used everywhere on a farm

Farms use water for drinking (people and animals), irrigation, mixing sprays, cleaning milking parlours and packhouses, and in hydroponics. Poor water quality can make people and animals sick, damage crops and soils, block irrigation systems, make sprays work badly and cause buyers to reject produce.

Sources of water

  • Boreholes – groundwater; may be salty or high in some minerals depending on the area.
  • Rivers and streams – can carry soil, sewage, fertiliser and chemicals from upstream.
  • Farm dams – can grow algae in warm weather; can be polluted by animals and runoff.
  • Municipal water – treated, but supply may be unreliable.
  • Rainwater tanks – usually clean but can be contaminated by dirty roofs or gutters.

What we check

MeasureWhat it tells you
pHHow acid or alkaline the water is; affects sprays, drippers and plant uptake
EC or TDS (salts)How salty the water is; high salts harm crops and soils and can affect animals
TurbidityCloudiness from soil particles; blocks filters and drippers, protects germs
E. coli / faecal bacteriaContamination from sewage or manure; a health risk for people and produce
NitratesOften from fertiliser or manure; high levels are a health risk
Hardness, ironCan form deposits that block drippers and reduce some sprays' effect

The target values depend on the use: drinking water for people, livestock water, irrigation water and water for washing fresh produce each have their own guidelines. The farm manager or advisor will tell you the targets to use.

Visual warning signs

  • Green scum or blue-green colour on a dam: possible toxic blue-green algae. Keep animals away and report at once.
  • Bad smell, foam or oily film.
  • Dead fish, frogs or birds near water.
  • Animals refusing to drink.

lessons.title: Sampling, testing and recording
lessons.html:
Taking water samples

A sample must represent the water being used, and must not be contaminated by the person taking it.

  1. Use the clean bottles from the laboratory. Bottles for bacteria tests are usually sterile; do not touch the inside or the lid.
  2. Label the bottle with the sample point, date, time and your name before you fill it.
  3. At a tap or borehole, let the water run for a few minutes first so you sample fresh water, not water that stood in the pipe.
  4. At a dam or river, take water away from the edge and below the surface, not the scum on top. Never take risks near deep water.
  5. Fill to the level the lab asks, close tightly.
  6. Keep samples cool and out of the sun, for example in a cooler box, and get them to the lab quickly. Bacteria samples in particular must reach the lab within the time the lab gives.

Testing on the farm

Some tests can be done on the farm with portable meters or test strips:

  • pH meter and EC meter – calibrate them as the instructions say, using the standard solutions, before use.
  • Test strips for some chemicals such as nitrates or chlorine.
  • Rinse probes with clean water after each test and store them as instructed.

Recording and reporting

Keep a water quality record for each sample point: date, sample point, test, result and who tested. Compare results with the targets. Report to your supervisor at once if a result is outside the target or if you see warning signs. Records over time show trends, for example a borehole slowly getting saltier.

Protecting water sources

  • Keep chemicals, fuel, manure heaps and toilets away from boreholes, rivers and dams.
  • Never wash spray tanks or rinse chemical containers in or near water.
  • Fence off sensitive areas where animals foul the water.
  • Keep borehole heads sealed and covered.

Key points

  • Poor water harms people, animals, crops, equipment and market access.
  • Check pH, salts, turbidity, bacteria and nitrates against targets for each use.
  • Sample with clean bottles, label first, and keep samples cool.
  • Calibrate meters and record every result.
  • Report problems and protect water sources from pollution.
